<reason>Both sides were strong and format-compliant, but A built the more tractable path under the motion's "more" standard. A's documented news-desert harms (borrowing costs, split-ticket decline) were plausibly grounded and never shown to be worse than the alternative; B's central harm was never instantiated and, by B4.1, became definitionally unobservable — which A's closing turned into a winning "unfalsifiable and proves too much" attack, since invisible self-censorship equally indicts private ownership. B's rebuttal craft was the sharpest in the debate (the auditor/judge disanalogy, the "different intervention" critique of the news-desert studies, "design answers a clause, not a workplace"), and B's internal critique — that the reductions require independence the funding severs — genuinely blunted A's benefits. But B never zeroed them: A's answers on deterrence running through records/prosecutors/rivals and on absence maximizing distrust survived. B also carried an unresolved tension: the subsidized paper must be distrusted enough to polarize yet believed enough to serve as a corruption alibi. With benefits only discounted, not destroyed, A's documented-current-compounding versus conditional-designable weighing carried the comparison.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's disanalogy of judges and inspectors general (their power doesn't require public belief; journalism has only belief) was the cleanest single hit and went largely unanswered. But the decisive exchange was A's Q1 demanding one captured firewalled newsroom → B's concession that capture is invisible ("the series that never starts") → A's closing reframing that as unfalsifiable and applicable to every funder, which shifted the epistemic burden back onto CON and let A's asymmetry weighing stand.</best_rebuttal>
